Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". - Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
**The Unsent**

We found them on the third day of clearing the house, in the bottom drawer of the rolltop desk, under a manual and a dead flashlight. A copy-paper box, the free kind, filled with envelopes. My sister pulled one out, read the front, handed it to me, and went on sorting.

My name, in his handwriting — the careful print he'd used on my lunch bags and my permission slips and, once, on the sign at my wedding: RESERVED. Every envelope was addressed to me. Every one had a stamp. Not one had been mailed.

There were a hundred and forty-six of them. We counted twice.

The earliest was dated June 4, 1981. I was four. The latest was dated the Tuesday before he died, eleven weeks ago. The stamps were wrong on half of them — too little postage, out-of-date rates — so he never checked. He wrote them knowing they would not go anywhere. He wrote them the way you talk into a pillow.

I took the box home. I told my sister I'd catalog them. I did not catalog them. I read them out of order, in the evenings, and then I started over and read them in order, and I will tell you some of what they said, because I have decided they were not private. Private is a word for things you're ashamed of. These were something else.

June 4, 1981: "You had a fever of 102 and I sat up with you and you asked me if the stars were hot. I said yes. You said, good, and went to sleep. I stayed up. I didn't know yet that I would keep staying up."

That's the fourth one. The first one is shorter. It says: "I am going to write these and not send them. I read about a man who did that. I don't remember where. It seemed useful."

A man in a magazine. That was the whole origin. My father, who did not finish college, who read the paper back to front and the manuals first, read about unsent letters in a magazine and started a thirty-eight-year correspondence with his daughter, postage due.

There is a letter for every B I cried over — he was not disappointed, he was terrified, there is a difference, he should have said so. There is a letter for the night I left for college, when he followed the car to the end of the driveway and then went inside and washed the car. "I washed a car that was already clean," he wrote. "Your mother pretended not to notice. She was good at that. I married her for it."

There is a letter about my wedding that I will not summarize except to say that he liked my husband more than he ever let on, and worried about him too, the way you worry about a boat you have watched leave the harbor.

There is a letter about the dog. There is a letter about the fight we had when I was thirty — I don't remember the fight, but he remembered it, he remembered my exact words, he had been carrying them. There is a letter that is only a recipe, for the chicken thing, the one I asked for at the hospital once and he said he'd write it down and never did. He wrote it down. He drew a diagram of the pan.

The handwriting changes in 1997. It gets smaller, tighter. He never told us about the tremor. There is a letter about the tremor.

The last ones are short. In March he wrote about the birds at the feeder, the finches that came in a pack of twelve, and how he had started naming them, all the same name. In April he wrote: "I am not afraid, exactly. I am annoyed. There is a difference. You taught me the difference, though you didn't mean to, when you were four and the stars were hot."

The last letter is dated the Tuesday before he died. It says: "Don't worry. I didn't send this. I never sent any of them. I want you to know that I knew what I was doing. I wasn't hiding. I was keeping. There is a difference, and I should have said so."

There is a difference, and he should have said so. That could be the epitaph. I have half a mind to put it on the stone.

Here is what I know now, or believe, which in my family is the same tense. Some people love out loud, and some people love in a copy-paper box at the bottom of a desk, and you don't get to choose which one you get, and you don't get to choose which one you are. He was not a man who talked into pillows. I take that back. He was a man who talked into a pillow for thirty-eight years and then labeled the pillow with my name and a stamp he never licked.

My sister thinks I should have them published. She thinks there is a book in them, a universal father. I told her no. Some correspondence is not for an audience. Some letters do their work by existing, the way a bridge does its work even when no one is on it.

But I did one thing. I took a legal pad — he would have liked that, the yellow, the lines — and I wrote him back. I told him about the finches at my own feeder, twelve of them, or maybe the same one twelve times. I told him the stars are hot, and that I stayed up. I told him about the chicken thing, that I made it, that the pan was wrong but it was close.

I addressed it to him. I put a stamp on it. I did not mail it. I put it in the box with the others, on top, the newest letter, the first reply.

It seemed useful.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A polished short story built around a dead father’s unsent letters and his daughter’s reply.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender and measured, letting grief emerge through practical details rather than grand declarations: a dead flashlight, incorrect postage, a washed car, a drawn diagram of a pan. The daughter’s discoveries reframe her father’s quietness as a form of keeping, without pretending that his silence caused no hurt. The story invites the reader to recognize how love can be present in forms that are hard to read until later.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds letters, handwriting, stamps, household tasks, and remembered phrases as containers for affection across time. It favors a moral distinction—“I wasn’t hiding. I was keeping”—and resolves the gap between father and daughter not by mailing a reply, but by placing it in the box with his.

## Evidence line
> Some people love out loud, and some people love in a copy-paper box at the bottom of a desk, and you don't get to choose which one you get, and you don't get to choose which one you are.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story’s recurring objects and carefully echoed phrases make its emotional design unusually coherent and distinctive.
